claim: LC axons in the cortex respond to unsigned visuomotor prediction errors.
source: Using two-photon calcium imaging in mice exploring a virtual environment, we found that the activity of LC axons in the cortex correlated with the magnitude of unsigned visuomotor prediction errors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging showing LC axonal responses to visuomotor mismatches and visual flow stimuli.

claim: LC response profiles are similar in both motor and visual cortical areas.
source: LC response profiles were similar in both motor and visual cortical areas, indicating that LC axons broadcast prediction errors throughout the dorsal cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing LC axonal responses between anterior (motor) and posterior (visual) cortical regions.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of LC axons facilitates learning of stimulus-specific suppression of visual responses during locomotion.
source: While imaging calcium activity in layer 2/3 of the primary visual cortex, we found that optogenetic stimulation of LC axons facilitated learning of a stimulus-specific suppression of visual responses during locomotion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from combined two-photon imaging and optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: LC-induced plasticity recapitulates the effect of visuomotor learning on a scale that is normally observed during visuomotor development across days.
source: This plasticity – induced by minutes of LC stimulation – recapitulated the effect of visuomotor learning on a scale that is normally observed during visuomotor development across days.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of optogenetically-induced plasticity with developmental plasticity data from coupled trained mice.

claim: Prediction errors drive LC activity.
source: We conclude that prediction errors drive LC activity, and that LC activity facilitates sensorimotor plasticity in the cortex, consistent with a role in modulating learning rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing LC responses to visuomotor mismatches and visual flow stimuli that scale with prediction error magnitude.

claim: LC activity facilitates sensorimotor plasticity in the cortex.
source: We conclude that prediction errors drive LC activity, and that LC activity facilitates sensorimotor plasticity in the cortex, consistent with a role in modulating learning rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that optogenetic LC stimulation enhances visuomotor plasticity.

claim: The brain learns to predict sensory feedback generated by movement through experience with the world.
source: Through experience with the world, brains learn to predict the sensory feedback generated by movement.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific understanding of sensorimotor learning.

claim: Learning the precise relationship between motor commands and resulting visual feedback is the basis for feedback control of movements and distinguishing self-generated from externally generated sensory feedback.
source: For instance, learning the precise relationship between motor commands and the resulting visual feedback is the basis for both feedback control of movements as well as distinguishing self-generated from externally generated sensory feedback.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific understanding of sensorimotor control.

claim: The brain may learn sensorimotor predictions via predictive processing.
source: One way that the brain may learn to do this is via predictive processing (Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018; Rao and Ballard, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: In predictive processing, the brain learns an internal model which transforms motor activity into a prediction of sensory consequences.
source: In a sensorimotor version of this framework, the brain learns an internal model which transforms motor activity into a prediction of the sensory consequences.
evidence: The claim describes a theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: Specific neurons compute prediction errors, which are discrepancies between predictions and actual sensory inputs.
source: The framework postulates that specific neurons are responsible for computing discrepancies – known as prediction errors – between the prediction and the actual sensory inputs received.
evidence: The claim describes a theoretical framework from predictive processing.

claim: The neocortex computes signals consistent with sensorimotor prediction errors.
source: The neocortex has been shown to compute signals consistent with sensorimotor prediction errors (Eliades and Wang, 2008; Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018; Schneider et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Excitatory neurons in layer 2/3 of V1 compute mismatches between visual flow speed and locomotion speed.
source: In the primary visual cortex (V1), excitatory neurons in layer 2/3 compute mismatches between visual flow speed and locomotion speed (Attinger et al., 2017; Jordan and Keller, 2020; Keller et al., 2012; Zmarz and Keller, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Sensorimotor prediction error responses in the cortex depend on ongoing and developmental experience with sensorimotor coupling.
source: Such sensorimotor prediction error responses in the cortex depend on ongoing and developmental experience with sensorimotor coupling (Attinger et al., 2017; Schneider et al., 2018; Vasilevskaya et al., 2022; Widmer et al., 2022), and therefore the computation underlying them is actively learned.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: In predictive processing, one main function of prediction errors is to drive corrective plasticity in the internal model that generates predictions.
source: In predictive processing, one main function of prediction errors is to drive corrective plasticity in the internal model that generates predictions (Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018).
evidence: The claim describes a theoretical framework supported by citation.

claim: During first sensorimotor experience, prediction errors should strongly drive learning of an internal model of the world.
source: During the first sensorimotor experience in life, prediction errors should strongly drive learning of an internal model of the world, while later in life, prediction errors should update internal models primarily when overall prediction errors are abundant (for instance, in novel or volatile situations).
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning about learning dynamics.

claim: Later in life, prediction errors should update internal models primarily when overall prediction errors are abundant.
source: During the first sensorimotor experience in life, prediction errors should strongly drive learning of an internal model of the world, while later in life, prediction errors should update internal models primarily when overall prediction errors are abundant (for instance, in novel or volatile situations).
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning about learning dynamics.

claim: A gating signal could implement developmental or contextual shifts in the amount of plasticity induced by a particular prediction error.
source: One way to implement such a developmental or contextual shift in the amount of plasticity induced by a particular prediction error would be a gating signal.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning about mechanisms for controlling plasticity.

claim: A gating signal is activated by prediction errors and permits increases in plasticity.
source: The characteristics of a gating signal are that it is activated by prediction errors and that it permits increases in plasticity.
evidence: The claim defines theoretical properties of a gating signal.

claim: A gating signal can be low dimensional because it is not driving plasticity but simply gating it.
source: In addition, because it is not driving plasticity, but simply gating it, it can be low dimensional (i.e. the same for all neurons).
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning about gating signals.

claim: Neuromodulatory systems are prime candidates for a gating signal.
source: Prime candidates for a gating signal are neuromodulatory systems.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the properties of neuromodulatory systems.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain signal reward prediction errors.
source: Dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain signal reward prediction errors (Kim et al., 2020; Schultz, 2016) and action prediction errors (Greenstreet et al., 2022), which are thought to gate plasticity in downstream targets to support learning of stimulus-reward associations and goal directed behavior (Cox and Witten, 2019; Flagel et al., 2011; Reynolds et al., 2001; Steinberg et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain signal action prediction errors.
source: Dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain signal reward prediction errors (Kim et al., 2020; Schultz, 2016) and action prediction errors (Greenstreet et al., 2022), which are thought to gate plasticity in downstream targets to support learning of stimulus-reward associations and goal directed behavior (Cox and Witten, 2019; Flagel et al., 2011; Reynolds et al., 2001; Steinberg et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Dopaminergic prediction errors are thought to gate plasticity in downstream targets to support learning of stimulus-reward associations and goal directed behavior.
source: Dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain signal reward prediction errors (Kim et al., 2020; Schultz, 2016) and action prediction errors (Greenstreet et al., 2022), which are thought to gate plasticity in downstream targets to support learning of stimulus-reward associations and goal directed behavior (Cox and Witten, 2019; Flagel et al., 2011; Reynolds et al., 2001; Steinberg et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Catecholamines regulate and gate plasticity in the cortex.
source: Indeed, the catecholamines – dopamine and noradrenaline – regulate and gate plasticity in the cortex (Choi et al., 2005; He et al., 2015; Seol et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: The midbrain dopaminergic system projects only sparsely to most of the sensory neocortex of the mouse, including V1.
source: However, the midbrain dopaminergic system projects only sparsely to most of the sensory neocortex of the mouse, including V1 (Nomura et al., 2014), where visuomotor predictions are thought to be learned (Attinger et al., 2017; Widmer et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical work.

claim: Visuomotor predictions are thought to be learned in V1.
source: However, the midbrain dopaminergic system projects only sparsely to most of the sensory neocortex of the mouse, including V1 (Nomura et al., 2014), where visuomotor predictions are thought to be learned (Attinger et al., 2017; Widmer et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: The locus coeruleus is the major catecholaminergic input to the cortex.
source: Instead, the major catecholaminergic input to the cortex is the locus coeruleus (LC).
evidence: The claim draws from established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The LC responds to unexpected task outcomes.
source: Such studies have shown that the LC responds to many different events, including unexpected task outcomes (Bouret and Sara, 2004; Breton-Provencher et al., 2022), novelty (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Vankov et al., 1995), and unexpected sensory stimuli in general (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981; Deitcher et al., 2019; Foote et al., 1980; Hervé-Minvielle and Sara, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: The LC responds to novelty.
source: Such studies have shown that the LC responds to many different events, including unexpected task outcomes (Bouret and Sara, 2004; Breton-Provencher et al., 2022), novelty (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Vankov et al., 1995), and unexpected sensory stimuli in general (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981; Deitcher et al., 2019; Foote et al., 1980; Hervé-Minvielle and Sara, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: The LC responds to unexpected sensory stimuli in general.
source: Such studies have shown that the LC responds to many different events, including unexpected task outcomes (Bouret and Sara, 2004; Breton-Provencher et al., 2022), novelty (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Vankov et al., 1995), and unexpected sensory stimuli in general (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981; Deitcher et al., 2019; Foote et al., 1980; Hervé-Minvielle and Sara, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: In zebrafish, noradrenergic neurons increase their activity during prolonged visuomotor mismatches of failed swim attempts to drive 'giving up' behavior.
source: In zebrafish, noradrenergic neurons increase their activity during the prolonged visuomotor mismatches of failed swim attempts to drive 'giving up' behavior (Mu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work in zebrafish.

claim: GCaMP6s positive cells in the LC are immunoreactive for tyrosine hydroxylase.
source: We confirmed that these injections labelled only cells in the LC, and that GCaMP6s positive cells were also immunoreactive for tyrosine hydroxylase, a marker for catecholaminergic neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Axonal fluorescence showed strong correlations with pupil diameter typical for LC axons.
source: Axonal fluorescence showed strong correlations with pupil diameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) typical for LC axons (Reimer et al., 2016), rapid responses to air puffs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) as previously reported (Breton-Provencher et al., 2022; Deitcher et al., 2019), and increases in fluorescence at locomotion onset that decayed during the locomotion bout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) consistent with earlier work (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citation to previous work.

claim: LC axons show rapid responses to air puffs.
source: Axonal fluorescence showed strong correlations with pupil diameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) typical for LC axons (Reimer et al., 2016), rapid responses to air puffs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) as previously reported (Breton-Provencher et al., 2022; Deitcher et al., 2019), and increases in fluorescence at locomotion onset that decayed during the locomotion bout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) consistent with earlier work (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citations to previous work.

claim: LC axons show increases in fluorescence at locomotion onset that decay during the locomotion bout.
source: Axonal fluorescence showed strong correlations with pupil diameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) typical for LC axons (Reimer et al., 2016), rapid responses to air puffs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) as previously reported (Breton-Provencher et al., 2022; Deitcher et al., 2019), and increases in fluorescence at locomotion onset that decayed during the locomotion bout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) consistent with earlier work (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: Within a field of view, individual LC axon segments exhibit highly correlated activity.
source: We found that within a FoV, individual axon segments exhibited highly correlated activity (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: LC axons show significant increases in fluorescence following mismatch presentations.
source: Indeed, LC axons showed significant increases in fluorescence following mismatch presentations (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C–D.

claim: Responses of LC axons to playback halts when the mouse was stationary were negative and substantially different from mismatch responses.
source: Responses of LC axons to playback halts when the mouse was stationary were negative and substantially different from mismatch responses (Figure 1C–D), demonstrating that the response of LC axons to visuomotor mismatch cannot be explained by the visual stimulus alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C–D.

claim: The response of LC axons to visuomotor mismatch cannot be explained by the visual stimulus alone.
source: Responses of LC axons to playback halts when the mouse was stationary were negative and substantially different from mismatch responses (Figure 1C–D), demonstrating that the response of LC axons to visuomotor mismatch cannot be explained by the visual stimulus alone.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing mismatch and playback halt responses.

claim: Mismatch responses were significantly larger than playback halt responses that occurred during locomotion in the open loop condition.
source: This indicated that responses in LC axons were acutely dependent on visuomotor coupling, since the only difference between a mismatch stimulus and a playback halt during locomotion is that the former occurs during visuomotor coupling and the latter does not.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing responses under different conditions.

claim: Responses in LC axons are acutely dependent on visuomotor coupling.
source: This indicated that responses in LC axons were acutely dependent on visuomotor coupling, since the only difference between a mismatch stimulus and a playback halt during locomotion is that the former occurs during visuomotor coupling and the latter does not.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing mismatch and playback halt responses during locomotion.

claim: LC axonal mismatch responses increase monotonically with the locomotion speed of the mouse.
source: Indeed, we found that LC axonal mismatch responses increased monotonically with the locomotion speed of the mouse (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: LC axonal responses to visuomotor mismatch are consistent with a visuomotor prediction error signal.
source: Thus, LC axonal responses to visuomotor mismatch are consistent with a visuomotor prediction error signal.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing speed-dependent responses.

claim: LC axons show significant responses to visual flow onsets, but only when the mouse is stationary.
source: We found that LC axons showed significant responses to visual flow onsets, but only when the mouse was stationary (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F–G.

claim: Visual flow onsets during locomotion did not evoke significant responses on average in LC axons.
source: Visual flow onsets during locomotion did not evoke significant responses on average.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on LC axonal responses.

claim: LC axonal responsiveness to visual and visuomotor stimuli is best explained by the absolute error between locomotion and visual flow speeds.
source: Altogether, LC axonal responsiveness to visual and visuomotor stimuli was best explained by the absolute (i.e. unsigned) error between locomotion and visual flow speeds (|Error|=|Speedlocomotion– Speedvisual flow|).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data across multiple stimulus conditions.

claim: LC axonal responses scale with the size of the change in unsigned error magnitude across different stimulus conditions.
source: Changes in the absolute error resulted in corresponding changes in the activity in LC axons (Figure 1C and F), and responses scaled with the size of Δ|Error| (i.e. the change in unsigned error magnitude, see Methods) across the different stimulus conditions (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, F, and H.

claim: Individual LC neurons can preferentially target different cortical areas.
source: Individual LC neurons can preferentially target different cortical areas (Chandler et al., 2019; Kebschull et al., 2016), but it is unclear whether these projection-specific neurons have differing response profiles.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical work.

claim: LC axons in anterior and posterior cortex show very similar responses to visuomotor mismatches, playback halts, visual flow onsets, air puffs, and locomotion onsets.
source: We found very similar responses to visuomotor mismatches, playback halts (stationary) and visual flow onsets (stationary; Figure 2B–C), as well as air puffs and locomotion onsets at these two locations (Figure 2B and D), and there were no significant differences in the responses between the two locations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–D.

claim: The LC sends similar visuomotor and locomotion related signals to distinct regions of the cortex.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that the LC sends similar visuomotor and locomotion related signals to distinct regions of the cortex, in line with recent findings showing that LC axons in different cortical regions show responses to the same sensory stimuli (Deitcher et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of ChrimsonR resulted in dilations of the right pupil in mice expressing ChrimsonR in a manner that depended on the degree of axon labelling.
source: Optogenetic stimulation, when presented in isolation, resulted in dilations of the right pupil in mice expressing ChrimsonR in a manner that depended on the degree of axon labelling (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), but not in control mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pupil dilation from optogenetic stimulation likely resulted from antidromic activation of the LC.
source: This likely resulted from antidromic activation of the LC, direct stimulation of which is known to produce strong ipsilateral pupil dilation (Liu et al., 2017), and increased our confidence that we were indeed driving LC axons with the parameters selected.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Onset of optogenetic stimulation caused a small calcium response across the population in ChrimsonR-expressing mice that was indistinguishable from that in control mice.
source: Onset of the optogenetic stimulation laser caused a small calcium response across the population in ChrimsonR-expressing mice, which was indistinguishable from that caused in control mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The small calcium response to optogenetic stimulation was likely due to a visual effect of the stimulation laser.
source: This was likely due to a visual effect of the stimulation laser.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similarity of responses in ChrimsonR and control mice.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of LC axons did not have a direct measurable effect on calcium activity of layer 2/3 neurons in V1.
source: The lack of a difference in this stimulation response between ChrimsonR-expressing mice and control mice indicated that optogenetic stimulation of LC axons did not have a direct measurable effect on calcium activity of L2/3 neurons in V1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing ChrimsonR and control mice.

claim: Responses to visual flow onsets appeared transiently more pronounced during laser stimulation in ChrimsonR-expressing mice only.
source: Responses to visual flow onsets (i.e. at the beginning of the visual flow stimulus, or at the offset of mismatch) appeared transiently more pronounced during laser stimulation in ChrimsonR-expressing mice only (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E–F.

claim: Averaging across the full response duration, there were no significant effects of laser stimulation on mismatch and visual flow responses.
source: However, this effect was small and not evident in average responses. Averaging across the full response duration, we found no significant effects of laser stimulation, both when comparing trials with and without laser stimulation in the ChrimsonR-expressing group, and when comparing the difference in response size between ChrimsonR-expressing and control mice (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E–F.

claim: There was no evidence for an effect of optogenetic stimulation of LC axons on average mismatch and visual flow responses across any functional cell groups.
source: We found no evidence for an effect of optogenetic stimulation of LC axons on average mismatch and visual flow responses across any of these cell groups (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G–H.

claim: Transient LC axon stimulation in the awake state has only a minor direct effect on the responses of neurons in layer 2/3 of V1.
source: We thus concluded that transient LC axon stimulation in the awake state has only a minor direct effect on the responses of neurons in layer 2/3 of V1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data on optogenetic stimulation effects.

claim: The results are largely in line with recent work demonstrating a lack of effect of LC stimulation on baseline firing in cortical pyramidal neurons, and an enhancement of transient responses to afferent input.
source: These results are largely in line with recent work demonstrating a lack of effect of LC stimulation on baseline firing in cortical pyramidal neurons, and an enhancement of transient responses to afferent input (Vazey et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The LC is thought to be involved in cortical plasticity.
source: The LC is thought to be involved in cortical plasticity (Kasamatsu et al., 1985; Kasamatsu and Pettigrew, 1976; Martins and Froemke, 2015; Shepard et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Catecholamine receptors in V1 modulate synaptic plasticity by activating intracellular signaling cascades and interacting with eligibility traces.
source: Catecholamine receptors in V1 are known to modulate synaptic plasticity by activating intracellular signaling cascades and interacting with eligibility traces (Choi et al., 2005; He et al., 2015; Nomura et al., 2014; Seol et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Primary sensory cortices can learn to suppress the sensory consequences of locomotion, driving selective reductions of responses to locomotion-coupled inputs.
source: Primary sensory cortices can indeed learn to suppress the sensory consequences of locomotion, driving selective reductions of responses to locomotion-coupled inputs (Schneider et al., 2018; Widmer et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In V1, there is a known increase in the size of visual responses during locomotion compared to stationary periods.
source: In V1, there is a known increase in the size of visual responses during locomotion compared to stationary periods (Bennett et al., 2013; Erisken et al., 2014; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Pakan et al., 2016; Polack et al., 2013; Zmarz and Keller, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The canonical gain increase of visual responses during locomotion was present for control mice but reversed in sign in ChrimsonR-expressing mice.
source: Analyzing only trials where the optogenetic stimulation laser was not on, we found that this canonical gain increase was present for control mice but reversed in sign in ChrimsonR-expressing mice: Visual responses during locomotion were suppressed on average relative to stationary periods (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: ChrimsonR-expressing mice had a significantly lower locomotion modulation index compared to control mice.
source: This resulted in a significantly lower locomotion modulation index (see Methods) for ChrimsonR-expressing relative to control mice (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The reversal of locomotion modulation index may reflect a result of plasticity induced by earlier LC axon stimulation.
source: Since episodic LC axon stimulation occurred throughout the whole imaging session (i.e. across 10 min in the closed loop condition, prior to the presentation of open loop visual flow stimuli), it is possible that the reversal of locomotion modulation index reflects a result of plasticity induced by earlier LC axon stimulation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental design and results.

claim: LC axon stimulation during closed loop visuomotor experience results in a significant reduction in the locomotion modulation index for nasotemporal visual flow responses.
source: Quantifying visual flow responses in high ChrimsonR-expressing mice after optogenetic stimulation during closed loop visuomotor experience revealed a significant reduction in the locomotion modulation index for nasotemporal visual flow responses (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The reduction in locomotion modulation index originated from a reduction in the response to visual flow during locomotion, while responses during stationary periods remained stable.
source: This originated from a reduction in the response to visual flow during locomotion, while responses during stationary periods remained stable (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The effect of LC stimulation on locomotion modulation index was specific to the direction of visual flow seen during forward locomotion.
source: This effect was specific to the direction of visual flow seen during forward locomotion, since locomotion modulation index was preserved for temporonasal visual flow responses (Figure 4D), with negligible changes in response size both during locomotion and stationary periods (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and H.

claim: The effect of LC stimulation on locomotion modulation index was specific to high ChrimsonR-expressing mice.
source: The effect was also specific to high ChrimsonR-expressing mice, as locomotion modulation index did not significantly change in both control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and low ChrimsonR-expressing mice (Figure 4E and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, Figure 4E, and Figure 4I.

claim: Stimulating LC axons during open loop replays drove a nonsignificant increase in locomotion modulation index for both nasotemporal and temporonasal visual flow responses.
source: Instead of a stimulus selective reduction in locomotion gain, this paradigm drove a nonsignificant increase in locomotion modulation index for both nasotemporal (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) and temporonasal visual flow (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The reduction in locomotion modulation index after stimulation of LC axons in the closed loop condition depends on visuomotor coupling experience.
source: This confirmed that the reduction in locomotion modulation index after stimulation of LC axons in the closed loop condition (Figure 4C) depends on visuomotor coupling experience and is not simply due to exposure to nasotemporal visual flow.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing closed loop and open loop stimulation conditions.

claim: LC axon stimulation over the course of minutes increases locomotion driven suppression of visual flow responses in layer 2/3 in a manner that is specific to reafferent stimulus properties and dependent on both ChrimsonR expression and visuomotor coupling.
source: We conclude that LC axon stimulation over the course of minutes increases locomotion driven suppression of visual flow responses in layer 2/3 in a manner that is specific to reafferent stimulus properties and dependent on both ChrimsonR expression and visuomotor coupling (Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data across multiple conditions shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The effect of LC stimulation on locomotion modulation could not be explained by differences in locomotion behavior between any of the groups analyzed.
source: Importantly, the effect could not be explained by differences in locomotion behavior between any of the groups analyzed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Visual flow responses were amplified during locomotion relative to stationary periods in normally reared mice but were suppressed during locomotion in coupled trained mice.
source: Analyzing responses to nasotemporal visual flow onsets during open loop replay, we found that visual flow responses were amplified during locomotion relative to stationary periods in normally reared mice but were suppressed during locomotion in coupled trained mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Coupled trained mice showed a significantly lower locomotion modulation index compared to normally reared mice.
source: This resulted in a significantly lower locomotion modulation index in coupled trained mice compared to normally reared mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The effect of coupled training on locomotion modulation index was not due to dark rearing.
source: The effect was not due to dark rearing, as non-coupled trained mice (also dark reared, but with only open loop virtual reality experience Figure 5A; Attinger et al., 2017) showed a positive locomotion modulation index on average that did not significantly differ from that of normally reared mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: As locomotion speed increased, visual flow responses were increasingly suppressed in coupled trained mice.
source: As locomotion speed increased, visual flow responses were increasingly suppressed in coupled trained mice (Figure 5D), while this was not evident in normally reared mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: After stimulation of LC axons in closed loop conditions, locomotion modulation index became increasingly negative as locomotion speed increased for nasotemporal visual flow responses in ChrimsonR-expressing mice.
source: For nasotemporal visual flow responses in ChrimsonR-expressing mice, locomotion modulation index was positive and did not change with locomotion speed at the start of the imaging session, but after stimulation of LC axons in closed loop conditions, locomotion modulation index became increasingly negative as locomotion speed increased (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F–G.

claim: The locomotion driven suppression of visual flow emerging after stimulating LC axons in closed loop conditions was locomotion speed dependent in a similar manner to the locomotion driven suppression seen in coupled trained mice.
source: Thus, the locomotion driven suppression of visual flow emerging after stimulating LC axons in closed loop conditions was locomotion speed dependent in a similar manner to the locomotion driven suppression seen in coupled trained mice.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing the speed dependence of suppression in the two groups.

claim: The pattern of differences in locomotion modulation was remarkably similar for ChrimsonR-expressing and coupled trained mice.
source: Overall, the pattern of differences in locomotion modulation was remarkably similar for ChrimsonR-expressing (Figure 5G, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) and coupled trained mice (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing experimental data across the two groups.

claim: The functional consequence of plasticity evoked by minutes of LC axon stimulation during visuomotor coupling is similar to that seen after experience is developmentally constrained to visuomotor coupling for days.
source: This indicates that the functional consequence of plasticity evoked by minutes of LC axon stimulation during visuomotor coupling is similar to that seen after experience is developmentally constrained to visuomotor coupling for days.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing the two experimental paradigms.

claim: The LC responds to unexpected stimuli of various modality, including reward prediction errors, punishment prediction errors, and novel or intense unexpected sensory stimuli.
source: The LC responds to unexpected stimuli of various modality, including reward prediction errors, punishment prediction errors, and novel or intense unexpected sensory stimuli (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981; Basu et al., 2022; Bouret and Sara, 2004; Breton-Provencher et al., 2022; Deitcher et al., 2019; Foote et al., 1980; Hervé-Minvielle and Sara, 1995; Su and Cohen, 2022; Takeuchi et al., 2016; Vankov et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The responses found in LC axons to various visual flow stimuli were proportional to the change in the degree of error between visual flow and locomotion speeds.
source: The responses we found in LC axons to the various visual flow stimuli were proportional to the change in the degree of error between visual flow and locomotion speeds (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Prediction errors of all modalities are a general feature of LC signaling.
source: This supports a model in which the LC signals prediction errors, and combined with previous findings, suggests that prediction errors of all modalities are a general feature of LC signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from current and previous findings.

claim: Both positive and negative visuomotor prediction errors appear to be computed in layer 2/3 of the primary visual cortex.
source: Both positive and negative visuomotor prediction errors appear to be computed in layer 2/3 of the primary visual cortex (Jordan and Keller, 2020) and activate the anterior cingulate cortex (Heindorf and Keller, 2022) – an area that projects directly to the LC.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The anterior cingulate cortex is activated by visuomotor prediction errors and projects directly to the LC.
source: Both positive and negative visuomotor prediction errors appear to be computed in layer 2/3 of the primary visual cortex (Jordan and Keller, 2020) and activate the anterior cingulate cortex (Heindorf and Keller, 2022) – an area that projects directly to the LC.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The LC likely inherits prediction errors computed upstream in areas like the cortex.
source: Thus, the LC likely inherits prediction errors computed upstream in areas like the cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from anatomical connectivity and functional data.

claim: The LC integrates prediction errors of all modalities to compute a measure of how inaccurately internal models are currently predicting the global sensory inputs of the animal.
source: Based on the multimodality and unsigned nature of LC responses, and the integrate and broadcast nature of its input-output anatomy (Schwarz et al., 2015), our working model of LC function is as follows: The LC integrates prediction errors of all modalities to compute a measure of how inaccurately internal models are currently predicting the global sensory inputs of the animal.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data and anatomical knowledge.

claim: The LC does not signal what type of prediction error occurred, but what the global rate of prediction errors currently is.
source: The LC does not signal what type of prediction error occurred, but what the global rate of prediction errors currently is (i.e. a measure of surprise).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The resulting LC output does not directly drive model updating in cortical output areas, but it modulates the rate at which local cortical prediction errors drive plasticity in internal models.
source: The resulting LC output does not directly drive model updating in cortical output areas, but it modulates the rate at which local cortical prediction errors drive plasticity in internal models.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The specificity of how internal models are changed depends on ongoing prediction errors in the cortex, and the LC input acts to control the learning rate.
source: Thus, the specificity of how internal models are changed depends on ongoing prediction errors in the cortex, and the LC input acts to control the learning rate, modulating the extent to which these cortical prediction errors drive plasticity.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data.

claim: When prediction error rates are high, updating of internal models will be more rapid as a result of increased LC output.
source: This would allow the LC to be a controller of plasticity in internal models: when prediction error rates are high (i.e. during developmental, novel, or volatile situations), updating of internal models will be more rapid as a result of increased LC output.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data.

claim: LC calcium responses to locomotion onsets were generally larger than visual flow or visuomotor mismatch responses.
source: LC calcium responses to locomotion onsets, which have been shown previously in LC axons (Deitcher et al., 2019; Reimer et al., 2016), were generally larger than visual flow or visuomotor mismatch responses (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and citations to previous work.

claim: Visuomotor prediction errors contribute to locomotion onset responses in LC axons.
source: We do find that visuomotor prediction errors contribute to locomotion onset responses, as locomotion onset responses in the open loop condition are smaller during visual flow, when locomotion evoked visuomotor error is lower (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LC calcium activity rises prior to locomotion onset.
source: However, LC calcium activity also rises prior to locomotion onset, creating the additional possibility of an internally generated movement onset response.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on LC activity time courses.

claim: Depleting noradrenaline has been shown to prevent forms of sensory-guided developmental plasticity in the cortex, including ocular dominance plasticity in V1.
source: Depleting noradrenaline has been shown to prevent forms of sensory-guided developmental plasticity in the cortex, including ocular dominance plasticity in V1 (Kasamatsu and Pettigrew, 1976) and changes in the tonotopic map in the auditory cortex (Shepard et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Depleting noradrenaline prevents changes in the tonotopic map in the auditory cortex.
source: Depleting noradrenaline has been shown to prevent forms of sensory-guided developmental plasticity in the cortex, including ocular dominance plasticity in V1 (Kasamatsu and Pettigrew, 1976) and changes in the tonotopic map in the auditory cortex (Shepard et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Acute noradrenergic receptor block can silence neurons in layer 2/3 and massively reduce the amplitude of visual inputs.
source: Indeed, acute noradrenergic receptor block can silence neurons in layer 2/3, and massively reduce the amplitude of visual inputs (Polack et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the LC has been shown to partially restore ocular dominance plasticity in adult cats.
source: In gain-of-function experiments, electrical stimulation of the LC has been shown to partially restore ocular dominance plasticity in adult cats (Kasamatsu et al., 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A few minutes of optogenetic LC axon stimulation in V1 of adult mice during visuomotor coupling can recapitulate the developmental effects of constrained exposure to visuomotor coupling in the virtual reality.
source: Here, we also performed a gain of function experiment: we show that a few minutes of optogenetic LC axon stimulation in V1 of adult mice during visuomotor coupling can recapitulate the developmental effects of constrained exposure to visuomotor coupling in the virtual reality (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation likely antidromically activates the LC owing to the resulting pupil dilation.
source: We know that we are likely antidromically activating the LC with our optogenetic stimulation owing to the resulting pupil dilation (Figures 3C and 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 4B.

claim: LC neurons are electrically coupled.
source: Given that LC neurons are electrically coupled (McKinney et al., 2022) and have widely divergent axons, our stimulation likely has effects on other LC output targets, such as other neuromodulatory systems, and other areas of the cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The plasticity effect measured may not entirely result from LC output in V1 alone.
source: Thus, the plasticity effect that we measure may not entirely result from LC output in V1 alone.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental design and anatomical knowledge.

claim: The functional impact of LC axon stimulation is strongly suggestive of a role in facilitating plasticity.
source: However, since the LC will never be acting in isolation and broadcasts its output to different cortical areas, the functional impact of LC axon stimulation in this experiment is strongly suggestive of a role in facilitating plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and anatomical knowledge.

claim: The plasticity occurs despite only minor effects of LC stimulation on neuronal activity.
source: The fact that the plasticity occurs despite only minor effects of LC stimulation on neuronal activity (Figure 3) indicates that the LC can either enhance plasticity without affecting activity levels, for instance via the molecular cascades or eligibility traces activated by GPCRs (He et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2022; Seol et al., 2007), and/or that a part of the relevant circuit outside of layer 2/3 is more strongly modulated by LC activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 3 and citations to previous work.

claim: Locus coeruleus activation has been shown to facilitate learning rates at the behavioral level.
source: Locus coeruleus activation has been shown to facilitate learning rates at the behavioral level (Glennon et al., 2023; Glennon et al., 2019; Martins and Froemke, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Learned suppression of reafferent visual flow during locomotion would theoretically be useful at the perceptual level for detection of external moving objects during movement.
source: This theoretically would be useful at the perceptual level for detection of external moving objects during movement, or for detecting changes in the geometry of the environment through which the animal is moving.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning about the function of the observed plasticity.

claim: Learned suppression of reafferent visual flow during locomotion would theoretically be useful for detecting changes in the geometry of the environment through which the animal is moving.
source: This theoretically would be useful at the perceptual level for detection of external moving objects during movement, or for detecting changes in the geometry of the environment through which the animal is moving.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical reasoning about the function of the observed plasticity.

claim: Prediction-error-driven catecholamine release is thought to gate cortical synaptic plasticity during reinforcement learning.
source: Prediction-error-driven catecholamine release is thought to gate cortical synaptic plasticity during reinforcement learning (He et al., 2015; Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A general function of catecholamines is to gate the plasticity underlying predictive learning across all modalities.
source: We propose that a general function of catecholamines is to gate the plasticity underlying predictive learning across all modalities.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from current and previous findings.
